newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Mary Robinson -- tipped for top human rights post.
newsitem.headline: Mary Robinson -- tipped for top human rights post.

text.p: Mary Robinson, Dublin's official nominee as the next U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, was Ireland's first woman head of state. Robinson, whose 1990 election broke new ground in a system where men had always held power, had announced on March 12 that she would not seek a second term in office when her presidential mandate expires later this year. "I have a sense of fulfilment in the position I hold now but I have a clear commitment to human rights and would like to continue in that area," Robinson told Irish television. On Wednesday, just one week later, the Irish government said that it was formally nominating Robinson to head the UNHCR and would "actively support her candidature in every possible way." The government's endorsement, which was expected, came as Robinson visited the U.N. criminal tribunal for former Yugoslavia in The Hague, the first head of state to do so. The White House encouraged her to seek the UNHCR job last weekend. A lawye

On the Irish stage a number of prominent names have been mentioned as possible successors to the popular president. They include former prime ministers Charles Haughey and Albert Reynolds, and Northern Ireland's John Hume. Hume, leader of the moderate nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), has become one of the best known spokesmen for moderate nationalism at home and abroad and is believed to be a popular cross-party choice.
Robinson, during her term in office, has injected new vibrancy into the presidency, refusing to follow in the track of earlier incumbents who were rarely seen and never heard.
A highly popular president, she kept a light burning at a window of her presidential home in the capital's Phoenix Park as a beacon to the "new Ireland" she championed.
Robinson's election as president ushered in a new era for a role that hitherto had been non-controversial, divorced from the ordinary people and kept behind closed doors.

Throwing open the doors of "Aras an Uachtarain", her state residence, she promoted "an inclusive Ireland" that sought to recognise the achievements and aspirations of groups that previously had been sidelined or silenced.

Minority groups, womens' and community associations, young people, Irish exiles and, crucially, ordinary Protestants and Catholics from beleaguered British Northern Ireland -- which she visited frequently -- were all made welcome.
She overcame odds of 1,000-1 in the male-dominated world of Irish politics to win the 1990 presidential election.
Once named "Man of the Year" in seaside Mayo where she was born in 1944, Robinson become Ireland's best ambassador.
She was an indefatigable globe-trotting traveller, clutching the hands of Somali famine victims, grieving for young boys killed by an IRA bomb, chatting with U.S. President Bill Clinton.
In May 1993 she met Britain's Queen Elizabeth, bridging seven centuries of mutual mistrust between Ireland and its former colonial master.

In June 1966 she travelled to Britain to meet the monarch again on the first official visit by a president of Ireland to its nearest neighbour. The visit reflected rapidly improved Anglo-Irish relations resulting from a bilateral bid to resolve years of conflict over Northern Ireland.
The visits underscored how Robinson, aware of the constitutional limitations of her job as a figurehead president, could make effective use of symbolism.
In a fiercely conservative and predominantly Roman Catholic land with some of the most draconian social laws in Europe, she has invited homosexuals and lesbians to her Dublin residence.
She offered the hand of friendship across the border to both sides of the sectarian divide in Northern Ireland where 3,200 people died in a 25-year conflict.
Robinson, an internationally respected civil rights lawyer backed by a coalition of left-wing groups, defeated the mighty Fianna Fail (Soldiers of Destiny) party in the election.

A member of the inner circle of former prime minister and Fianna Fail leader Albert Reynolds paid her the ultimate compliment, telling the Irish Times: "The woman has the job and she's playing a blinder. She is the best ambassador we have got."
